subject: Climate & Environment
title: How the Ocean Becomes Acidic
description: One-minute skill: How the Ocean Becomes Acidic.

hook.text: The ocean isn't turning to acid. But a 30% increase in acidity is already reshaping marine life.

buildup.text: When CO₂ dissolves in seawater, it forms carbonic acid. More CO₂ means more acid.

discovery.text: Ocean pH has dropped from 8.2 to 8.1 since preindustrial times. That's a 30% acidity increase.

twist.text: The pH scale is logarithmic. A small number change represents a huge chemical shift.

climax.text: If emissions continue, ocean pH could fall another 0.3 units by 2100 — unprecedented in 300 million years.

punchline.text: The ocean is absorbing our CO₂. The chemistry is changing.

quiz.question: What causes ocean acidification?
options: CO₂ dissolving in seawater forms carbonic acid
Industrial chemicals dumped in the ocean
Volcanic eruptions on the sea floor

details.summary: When CO2 dissolves in seawater it forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions and lowers pH. Ocean acidity has risen about 30 percent since preindustrial times. This chemical shift reduces the availability of carbonate ions that corals and shellfish need to build their structures.
details.whyItMatters: Acidification undermines the foundation of marine food webs. Organisms that build calcium carbonate shells or skeletons become vulnerable, with cascading effects throughout ocean ecosystems.
takeaways: CO2 dissolving in seawater forms carbonic acid and lowers pH
Ocean acidity has increased roughly 30 percent since the 1800s
Reduced carbonate ions weaken shells and coral skeletons

faq.question: How is ocean acidity measured?
faq.answer: Acidity is measured on the pH scale. Before industrialization, average ocean pH was about 8.2. It has since dropped to about 8.1, which represents a 30 percent increase in hydrogen ion concentration because the scale is logarithmic.

faq.question: Which marine organisms are most at risk from acidification?
faq.answer: Organisms that build calcium carbonate structures are most vulnerable: corals, mollusks like oysters and clams, sea urchins, and tiny pteropods. These creatures struggle to form and maintain shells as carbonate saturation decreases.
